extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology and creative-writing; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and categorizing narratorial position, focalization, non-narrative comments, and descriptive strategies in fictional texts; guidance for identifying how narrator, focalizer, and actors relate and how description/argumentation function rhetorically. Useful for literary analysis and informed creative-writing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish narrator, focalizer, and actor (agent identities and coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which of the three narrative agents (narrator, focalizer, actor) are distinct or coincide; use notation to record coincidences (e.g., CN (Ott.) [CF (Ott.)-Steyn]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sentence can be parsed as (I narrate: (I state autobiographically in order to explain:)) Steyn’s deep bass resounded in the vestibule. Two of the three agents may share the same identity (narrator and focalizer both Ottilie) while the actor differs (Steyn). Record coincidences because they affect interpretation (partiality, truth-claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptible vs non-perceptible narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the narrator manifests itself perceptibly in the text (e.g., names itself as 'I') or remains imperceptible/anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark narrator as perceptible (p) or non-perceptible (np) in shorthand (e.g., EN(np) [EF1 [cF2 (Ott.)]-Steyn(p)]). A perceptible 'I' need not be a fabula-character; perceptibility affects how presence, witness-status, and truth-claims are read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as witness (testimonial narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when the narrator functions as a witness: an 'I' who testifies about events and may be present at the scene or report having obtained information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A witness can remain invisible yet committed, convey compassion or irony, influence veracity, and raise ethical questions (modesty vs voyeurism). If the narrator claims a source (e.g., Steyn himself), note how it legitimizes testimonial status and affects implied truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded / double focalization (levels of focalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect cases where focalization is layered: an external focalizer embedding a character-bound focalizer (double focalization) or other multi-level focalization arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use level notation (e.g., EF1 [cF2 (Ott.)]-Steyn). Embedded focalization signals partiality and can create infiltration of external agents into the story; analyze which level supplies perception, partiality, or judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidence and displacement of narrative functions (narrating, perceiving, acting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Map whether the narrative 'I' exclusively narrates, also perceives, and/or acts; identify combinations and note changes over the text (continuity vs displacement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example distinctions: a narrative 'I' may narrate only (d), perceive (e/f/g), or act (e/g), and when it acts the action may be limited to testimony. The traditional 'I' vs 'he' distinction is inadequate; track infiltration of 'I' into story and temporal changes in narrative situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived truth-claim and fictionality signalled by narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how a narrator's stance and self-presentation (e.g., claiming to be perceptible/most truthful) signals a truth-claim or guarantees fictionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may adopt EN(p) position to assert truthfulness (Don Quixote examples). Distinguish between factual truth and an implied claim by the narrator about veracity; such claims shape reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of focalization and reader misreading of consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether focalization is consistently maintained and how extreme consistency may invite misinterpretation of anonymous agents as specific characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: La jalousie (Robbe-Grillet) maintains EN(np) narration and CF focalization so consistently that critics infer a specific character (jealous husband). Note that technical consistency can produce interpretive effects external to the text's formal scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-person narration viability and deixis (limits of 'you')
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether second-person narration functions as genuine second-person deixis or collapses into first-person subjectivity for readers; evaluate manageability for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Butor’s La modification shows the second person often reverts into an 'I' in practice; second-person lacks reversibility (the exchange of I/you) required by deixis and is difficult to sustain as a stable narrative situation. Consider deixis theory (Benveniste) and whether the 'you' can be the reader's counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate narrative and non-narrative comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between sentences that narrate fabula-events and those that are non-narrative comments (argumentative, descriptive, or general statements outside the fabula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze alternation between narration and non-narrative comments to uncover overt ideology. Example: Danny Goes Shopping lines 9–15 contain opinions ('fortunately') and catechistic Q&A that function argumentatively rather than narratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify argumentative textual passages (ideological statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize argumentative sentences that refer to general knowledge or opinions outside the fabula (broadly 'argumentative' in the widest sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative includes opinions and declarations (e.g., 'water boils at 100 degrees', 'Poland lies behind the Iron Curtain'). Such statements often communicate ideology; distinguish between factual claims and dated/opinionated statements when evaluating tenor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate discursive form and its ideological effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how discursive form (catechistic Q&A, exclamations, drills) shapes ideology and persuasion within a narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms like mock dialogue or repeated catechism render opinions self-evident and naturalize cultural norms (e.g., marriage as the natural consequence of love). Examine punctuation, rhetorical framing, and presentation-as-self-evident as ideological devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description as a privileged site of focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat descriptive passages as central locales for focalization and ideological/aesthetic effect; descriptions make fabula elements visible and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description attributes features to objects and enables reader participation in imagining the fictional world. Because description interrupts the fabula line, analyze how it is motivated and integrated with focalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimit description (definition and mixture with narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a description as a textual fragment in which features are attributed to objects; recognize mixtures where description and narration overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dickens passage (b) attributes features but also accounts for time passage — label as a mixture. Consider whether the descriptive function dominates to categorize as description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation of description (speaking, looking, acting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that descriptive interruptions be motivated by speaking, looking, or acting; motivation makes description believable within realist rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation through looking (focalization) is most frequent and subtle: the character's perception supplies time and reason to look. Exterior motivations (light, window, time) must be considered. Also distinguish subjective (character's abundant time) vs exterior motivation, and note when action itself incorporates description (Homeric instances, Zola polishing locomotive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric of description: components and relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze rhetorical means by which description masks arbitrariness: identify theme and sub-themes, predicates (qualifying vs functional), and trope relations (metaphor, synecdoche, metonymy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Themes = objects (house), sub-themes = components (door, roof); predicates qualify ('pretty') or functionally describe ('inhabitable for six'). Relations: synecdoche (part for whole), contiguity (= metonymy), metaphorical replacement. Use these categories to read rhetorical effect and ideological masking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 1 — Referential/encyclopaedic description
rubrics_metrics.description: A description with no figures of speech; selection based on contiguity of components; objective is to convey knowledge (encyclopaedic model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of some elements implies absence of others; reader expected to fill missing detail. Use for neutral, informative depictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 2 — Referential-rhetorical description
rubrics_metrics.description: Units combined by contiguity and thematic/evaluative function (tourist-guide model); objective both to convey knowledge and to persuade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasion via wording (rhythm/style), choice of valued sub-themes, and evaluative predicates. Even with metaphors, contiguity principle often remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 3 — Metaphoric metonymy
rubrics_metrics.description: Contiguity still dominates, but each component is rendered as a metaphor; comparing elements may replace components and require readers to fill-in implicit content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficially incoherent descriptions rely on reader's filling-in activity; reading involves reconstruction of omitted components implied by comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 4 — Systematized metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole description functions as one large metaphor with systematically related series (compared elements and compared-to elements), built on contiguity principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two series balance each other; dominance depends on context. Often elements of each series imply elements of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 5 — Metonymic metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: A large metaphor whose elements are contiguously related so the whole description is the comparison; relation may be implicit and indistinguishable out of context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit comparing element produces Homeric comparison; otherwise the type can be mistaken for other description types when decontextualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 6 — Series of metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A description built from a repeated, expanding metaphor adjusted to suggest that the compared element is elusive and indescribable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated adjustments create impression of elusiveness; useful for modernist/decadent styles emphasizing ineffability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptology in practice (integrating rhetoric, metaphor, and narrativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, descriptive passages often blend metaphor, decentring evocation, and narrativity; assess how rhetoric (expansion, ekphrasis, anticipation) both stops narrative and intensifies moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Djuna Barnes Nightwood passage uses metaphor, ekphrasis, deceleration, and anticipatory foresight: description both interrupts the story and signals thematic/critical meaning. Note interplay of narrator perspective and rhetorical devices when evaluating effect.
